entities.name: Saud al-Kabeer
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saud bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, known to history as Saud al-Kabeer or "Saud the Great," reigned as the second Imam of the First Saudi State from 1803 until his death in 1814. His eleven-year rule marked the zenith of the nascent Saudi polity's power and territorial expansion, transforming it from a regional emirate into a formidable force that directly challenged Ottoman suzerainty over the Arabian Peninsula. By successfully annexing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, Saud al-Kabeer not only expanded his domain but also claimed the prestigious title of 'Servant of the Two Holy Cities,' a significant spiritual and political assertion that profoundly reshaped the religious and geopolitical landscape of West Asia.

Upon succeeding his father, Abdulaziz ibn Muhammad, Saud al-Kabeer immediately embarked on a series of aggressive military campaigns designed to consolidate and extend Saudi influence. In 1803, his forces captured Mecca, followed by Medina in 1805, dismantling centuries of Ottoman control over the Hijaz and disrupting the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Under his command, the Saudi army pushed northward into Syria and Iraq, conducting raids that reached as far as Damascus and the outskirts of Baghdad, and eastward into Oman. These military successes were underpinned by the rigorous application of Wahhabi doctrines, which provided ideological unity and martial fervor to his tribal levies, enabling the Saudis to control the majority of the Arabian Peninsula by 1807.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saud al-Kabeer's reign expanded the First Saudi State to its greatest extent, capturing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina and directly challenging Ottoman authority, thereby instigating a major regional war and laying foundational claims for the modern Saudi state.
